ECE 6390 / Exam 1

Read the Mission as One Connected Calculation

Fig. 1 shows why the first-exam topics belong together. A spacecraft has to be in a useful place, stay operable there, aim a radio signal, and supply a receiver with enough usable power. Every later calculation needs an earlier choice stated clearly.

Start with Chapters I and II: position and motion become radius, speed, visibility, slant range, elevation and azimuth. Chapter III asks how power, stored energy, attitude, propulsion and heat keep that link operating. Chapters IV and V connect currents and traveling fields to directional radiation, receiving area and polarization. Chapter VI closes the chain by comparing received carrier power with the losses and noise at a declared receiver plane.

For each figure, keep track of the observer and the measured quantity. A geocentric radius starts at Earth’s center; a station’s look-angle ray starts at the ground. Coherent signals can cancel at a receiver, so add their field or voltage amplitudes with phase. For uncorrelated noise sources, the cross terms average to zero and their mean powers add. A battery stores energy, while an RF transmitter consumes electrical power and radiates only part of it. These distinctions determine which equation can answer the question.

The worked examples use independent teaching inputs. Follow the GEO station from Fig. 14 to the receiver calculation at Fig. 51 to see why a satellite above the horizon can still fall short of the required carrier-to-noise ratio.

Practice

1. Double the range while keeping frequency, power, gains and excess losses fixed. How do received power and free-space path loss change?

Use the inverse-square range dependence and 20 log10 of the range ratio.

Received power becomes one quarter, about 6.02 dB lower. Free-space path loss increases by about 6.02 dB. Receiver noise is unchanged if its temperature and equivalent bandwidth are unchanged.
